extracted.intended_audience: aspiring middle-grade authors, educators, librarians, and young-writer mentors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating middle-grade books (especially fantasy/mythology) that engage 8–12-year-old readers, including craft tips, audience-sensitivity, accessibility, and series planning. Emphasizes reading, practice, persistence, and listening to kids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read, practice, and persist
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three key tips to becoming a writer — read, practice, and persist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read widely to learn what works; keep writing to improve craft; persist through rejection and setbacks. (Direct, high-level advice presented as Riordan's core prescription for aspiring writers.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the middle-grade sensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A former middle school English and History teacher... talks about having the right sensibility to understand and write for the middle grade-aged kids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that middle-grade years involve many transitions — social, emotional, intellectual, and physical — and that books should speak to those specific experiences and needs of that age group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make books that speak to kids' experiences (be engaging and take them seriously)
rubrics_metrics.description: All kids wanted the same things from their teachers — engagement, passion, and someone who cared about them and took them seriously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write compelling books that treat middle-grade readers seriously; prioritize engagement (pace, stakes, relatable concerns) and convey passion for the subject to hold their attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let kids be the final arbiters (listen to reader response)
rubrics_metrics.description: For him, though, the final arbiters for his books are the kids and he is awed by the passion his work is inspiring in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use young readers' reactions and questions to judge whether stories are working and to guide decisions (for example, expanding a series when readers express demand).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fantasy and mythology to hook reluctant readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Rick Riordan didn’t like to read as a child … until he found the right books. Once he discovered fantasy fiction he was hooked. His eighth grade teacher introduced him to The Lord of the Rings, a book inspired by Norse mythology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporating mythic elements and fantasy can engage readers who otherwise resist reading; leveraging familiar myth structures can provide entry points for middle graders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write with accessibility for learners with ADHD/dyslexia in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Rick Riordan never intended to write a children’s book. But then learning differences caused his second grade son to hate reading and writing. But he loved Greek Mythology and Percy Jackson and the Lightning Thief was born.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider readability, pacing, and character hooks that help readers with learning differences engage (Riordan cites personal motivation to reach kids with ADHD/dyslexia). Craft choices that lower barriers to entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote and publish underrepresented voices inspired by folklore and mythology
rubrics_metrics.description: He started his own imprint ‘Rick Riordan Presents’ with the goal of publishing great middle grade authors from underrepresented cultures and backgrounds, to let them tell their own stories inspired by the mythology and folklore of their own heritage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support authentic cultural perspectives and allow authors from those communities to retell/reshape their own mythologies; center cultural specificity and authenticity in submissions and acquisitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan series structure but remain responsive to readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Author Rick Riordan knew from the beginning he wanted to make Percy Jackson a series, but he always had a 5 book length in mind. Thanks to questions from kids, though, he realized there were still more stories to tell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have an overarching series plan (e.g., planned number of books/arc) but be open to extending or adapting the series based on story needs and reader interest; use reader engagement as a signal for continuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a teacherly mindset toward young readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Riordan was a middle school English teacher who learned that all kids wanted the same things from their teachers — engagement, passion, and someone who cared and took them seriously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring the empathy, clarity, and enthusiasm of a good teacher into writing: explain stakes clearly, create accessible entry points, and respect the intelligence and emotional life of middle-grade readers.
